questions.scenario: A small company with limited data (500 labeled examples) wants to build a text classifier. Training a model from scratch on 500 examples would severely overfit.
questions.stem: Which approach leverages knowledge from large pre-trained models to overcome limited data?

options.text: Collect 500,000 more labeled examples before attempting any model training
Use transfer learning — start from a pre-trained model that already understands language and fine-tune it on the 500 examples
Train a rule-based system instead since ML requires millions of examples
Increase model size to compensate for limited data

explanation.correct: Transfer learning starts from a model pre-trained on massive data, carrying over learned representations (grammar, semantics, reasoning). Fine-tuning on 500 examples adapts these representations to the specific task, requiring far less task-specific data.

distractors.A: Collecting 500,000 examples is often impractical for small companies. Transfer learning specifically addresses the limited-data scenario.
distractors.C: ML with transfer learning works well with limited labeled data. Rule-based systems are inflexible and don't generalize like neural models.
distractors.D: Larger models with limited data overfit more, not less. Transfer learning addresses the knowledge gap, not model capacity.

questions.scenario: A team wants to fine-tune a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock without managing training infrastructure. They have their labeled dataset in S3.
questions.stem: What does Amazon Bedrock provide for this fine-tuning workflow?

options.text: Only pre-built models with no customization capability
A managed fine-tuning service that accepts training data and produces a custom model without requiring infrastructure management
GPU instances that the team must configure, monitor, and manage themselves
Only prompt engineering tools with no weight modification capability

explanation.correct: Amazon Bedrock provides managed fine-tuning — you supply training data and configuration, and Bedrock handles the training infrastructure, producing a custom model accessible through the same API without infrastructure management.

distractors.A: Bedrock supports both base and custom (fine-tuned) models. Customization through fine-tuning is a core capability.
distractors.C: Bedrock is fully managed. You don't provision or manage GPU instances — that's what SageMaker custom training jobs require.
distractors.D: Bedrock supports both prompt engineering and fine-tuning. Custom models with modified weights are available alongside prompt-only usage.

questions.scenario: A team prepares fine-tuning data for a customer intent classifier. Their initial 2,000 examples contain 1,800 'billing inquiry' labels and only 200 spread across 9 other categories.
questions.stem: What risk does this data distribution create for fine-tuning?

options.text: The model will learn to predict 'billing inquiry' disproportionately because the training signal is dominated by that class
The model will refuse to learn the billing category because it appears too frequently
Class imbalance only affects pre-training, not fine-tuning
The model will automatically balance the classes internally without any data adjustment

explanation.correct: Imbalanced training data biases the model toward the majority class. The gradient updates during fine-tuning are dominated by billing examples, causing the model to under-learn minority categories and over-predict billing.

distractors.B: Models learn what they see most. High frequency reinforces the pattern — it doesn't cause rejection of that category.
distractors.C: Class imbalance affects any supervised learning phase, including fine-tuning. The model learns from the distribution it's shown.
distractors.D: Models don't automatically balance classes. Without explicit techniques (oversampling, class weights, balanced batches), the model reflects training distribution.

questions.scenario: A data science team wants to fine-tune an open-source foundation model on their domain data. They need GPU cluster management, distributed training support, and the ability to customize training scripts.
questions.stem: Which AWS service provides this level of training infrastructure control?

options.text: Amazon Bedrock — fully managed with no infrastructure access
Amazon S3 — object storage for training data
AWS Lambda — serverless compute for training workloads
Amazon SageMaker with JumpStart — provides configurable training infrastructure, pre-built algorithms, and custom script support for fine-tuning FMs

explanation.correct: SageMaker with JumpStart provides infrastructure control for fine-tuning — GPU cluster management, distributed training, custom training scripts, and pre-built fine-tuning algorithms for foundation models from the model hub.

distractors.A: Bedrock is fully managed — you don't access training infrastructure directly. SageMaker provides the infrastructure control this team needs.
distractors.B: S3 stores training data but provides no compute, no training orchestration, and no GPU management for fine-tuning.
distractors.C: Lambda has execution time limits (15 min) and no GPU support. It cannot handle the hours-long GPU-intensive workloads of fine-tuning.

questions.scenario: A team needs to fine-tune a 70B parameter model but only has access to a single GPU with 24GB of VRAM — insufficient to fit the full model in memory for training.
questions.stem: Which technique allows fine-tuning this model within their memory constraints?

options.text: Increase the batch size to process more examples per step
Use full fine-tuning with gradient checkpointing only
Convert the model to a CPU-only training configuration
LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) — freeze most parameters and train only small low-rank matrices, dramatically reducing memory requirements

explanation.correct: LoRA freezes all original parameters and adds small trainable low-rank matrices to specific layers. Only these small matrices need gradients stored in memory, reducing VRAM requirements from hundreds of GB to a fraction — enabling single-GPU fine-tuning of large models.

distractors.A: Larger batch sizes increase memory usage. This would worsen the memory constraint, not solve it.
distractors.B: Gradient checkpointing helps but may not sufficiently reduce memory for a 70B model on 24GB. LoRA's parameter reduction is more effective.
distractors.C: CPU training is orders of magnitude slower and doesn't solve the fundamental memory constraint for storing activations during training.

questions.stem: Which statements correctly describe how transfer learning benefits downstream tasks? (Select TWO)

options.text: Pre-trained representations capture general language understanding that transfers to specific tasks, reducing the amount of task-specific data needed
Fine-tuning a pre-trained model typically converges faster than training from random initialization because the starting weights already encode useful patterns
Transfer learning eliminates the need for any task-specific training data
Transfer learning only works when source and target tasks are in the same language
Transfer learning always produces worse results than training from scratch

explanation.correct: Pre-trained representations reduce data requirements because the model already understands language structure. Training also converges faster since weights start from a useful initialization rather than random values.

distractors.C: Transfer learning reduces but doesn't eliminate data needs. Some task-specific examples are still needed to adapt the model.
distractors.D: Multilingual models demonstrate cross-lingual transfer. Transfer learning works across languages, not just within one language.
distractors.E: Transfer learning typically outperforms training from scratch, especially with limited data. That's its primary advantage.

questions.scenario: A team is preparing training data for fine-tuning their model on a technical support task.
questions.stem: Which data quality factors most impact fine-tuning effectiveness? (Select THREE)

options.text: Label accuracy — incorrectly labeled examples teach the model wrong patterns
Distribution coverage — examples must represent the variety of inputs the model will encounter in production
Example quality — poorly written or ambiguous examples produce unclear learning signals
File format — data must be stored in exactly 3 specific file formats
Time of creation — data created on weekdays produces better models than weekend data
Author credentials — only PhDs can produce valid training examples

explanation.correct: Label accuracy ensures correct supervision signals. Distribution coverage ensures the model encounters the full input variety. Example quality ensures clear, unambiguous learning signals. All directly impact what the model learns.

distractors.D: Multiple formats are supported (JSONL, CSV, etc.). No restriction to exactly 3 specific formats affects model quality.
distractors.E: Data creation time has no impact on training quality. Content and labeling accuracy are what matter.
distractors.F: Domain expertise helps with quality, but anyone can create valid training examples if they understand the task and produce accurate labels.

questions.scenario: An architect is evaluating Amazon Bedrock's fine-tuning capabilities for their organization.
questions.stem: What does Amazon Bedrock's managed fine-tuning provide? (Select TWO)

options.text: Handles training infrastructure automatically — no GPU provisioning, cluster management, or distributed training configuration needed
Produces custom models accessible through the same Bedrock API as base models
Requires teams to write custom training loops and optimizer code
Only supports fine-tuning Amazon Titan models, not third-party models
Provides direct SSH access to training instances for debugging

explanation.correct: Bedrock manages all training infrastructure (no GPU management needed) and produces custom models served through the standard Bedrock API alongside base models — a fully managed fine-tuning experience.

distractors.C: Bedrock is fully managed. You provide data and configuration — Bedrock handles training code, optimization, and infrastructure.
distractors.D: Bedrock supports fine-tuning for multiple model providers available in its catalog, not just Amazon Titan.
distractors.E: Bedrock is serverless — there are no instances to SSH into. Training is fully abstracted from the user.

questions.stem: What are characteristics of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA? (Select THREE)

options.text: Only a small number of additional parameters are trained while the base model remains frozen
Multiple task-specific adapters can share the same frozen base model, enabling multi-task deployment
Memory requirements are dramatically reduced compared to full fine-tuning since gradients are only computed for the small trainable subset
PEFT always produces higher accuracy than full fine-tuning on every benchmark
PEFT eliminates the need for labeled training data entirely
PEFT requires more GPU memory than full fine-tuning due to adapter overhead

explanation.correct: PEFT trains few parameters (efficient), enables adapter sharing on frozen models (multi-task flexibility), and reduces memory by only computing gradients for the small trainable subset.

distractors.D: Full fine-tuning sometimes outperforms PEFT because it optimizes all parameters. PEFT trades some peak performance for efficiency.
distractors.E: PEFT still requires labeled data for supervised training. It's efficient in compute, not data-free.
distractors.F: PEFT uses dramatically less memory than full fine-tuning. Adapters are tiny compared to the full model's gradient memory requirements.

questions.stem: How does multitask fine-tuning differ from single-task fine-tuning in its effect on the model? (Select TWO)

options.text: It trains on examples from multiple task types simultaneously, producing a model capable of following diverse instructions
It reduces catastrophic forgetting because the diverse training signal prevents weights from over-specializing to one domain
It requires less total training data than single-task fine-tuning
It produces a model that can only perform the tasks included in training and nothing else
It eliminates the need for pre-training since multiple tasks provide enough learning signal

explanation.correct: Multitask fine-tuning trains across diverse tasks simultaneously, producing instruction-following models. The variety prevents over-specialization, maintaining general capability — directly mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

distractors.C: Multitask fine-tuning typically requires MORE total data (examples across all tasks). Its benefit is capability breadth, not data efficiency.
distractors.D: Instruction-tuned models generalize to new instructions beyond their training tasks. They follow the pattern of instruction-following, not just memorized tasks.
distractors.E: Multitask fine-tuning still requires a pre-trained base model. Pre-training provides the foundational language understanding that fine-tuning builds upon.

questions.scenario: A startup wants to fine-tune a model for their specific use case. They compare Amazon Bedrock's managed fine-tuning with doing it themselves on SageMaker.
questions.stem: What is the PRIMARY tradeoff between Bedrock managed fine-tuning and SageMaker custom training?

options.text: Bedrock is always cheaper regardless of the workload
SageMaker cannot fine-tune foundation models — only Bedrock supports this
Bedrock fine-tuning produces better models than SageMaker in all cases
Bedrock provides simplicity with less control, while SageMaker provides full infrastructure control with more operational responsibility

explanation.correct: Bedrock abstracts infrastructure (simple but less customizable). SageMaker gives full control over training scripts, hyperparameters, distributed training, and instance types — but requires managing that complexity.

distractors.A: Cost depends on workload. SageMaker spot instances or specific configurations may be cheaper for certain use cases.
distractors.B: SageMaker with JumpStart fully supports fine-tuning foundation models with more customization options than Bedrock.
distractors.C: Model quality depends on data and configuration, not the platform. Both can produce equivalent results with proper setup.

questions.scenario: A team fine-tunes a sentiment classifier. Their test set shows 95% accuracy. However, in production, accuracy drops to 72%. Investigation reveals the training data was all formal product reviews, while production inputs include slang, abbreviations, and multilingual text.
questions.stem: What data preparation failure caused this production performance gap?

options.text: The training data had too many examples
The model was over-parameterized for the sentiment task
Training distribution did not match production distribution — formal reviews don't represent the informal, multilingual inputs encountered in deployment
The test set was too large, causing overfitting during evaluation

explanation.correct: Training-production distribution mismatch is a fundamental data preparation failure. The model learned patterns from formal text and cannot generalize to informal/multilingual inputs it never saw during fine-tuning.

distractors.A: More examples typically improve performance. The issue is distribution mismatch, not quantity.
distractors.B: Over-parameterization could cause overfitting but wouldn't explain the specific mismatch between formal training and informal production data.
distractors.D: Test set size doesn't cause overfitting. Overfitting occurs during training, not evaluation.

questions.stem: What concept explains why so few French examples produced a capable model?

options.text: Sequential transfer learning — each training phase transfers knowledge to the next, so the French model benefits from both pre-training knowledge and English sentiment understanding
The model memorized all 100 French examples and repeats them verbatim
French and English are identical languages at the token level
100 examples is always sufficient for any task regardless of complexity

explanation.correct: Transfer learning stacks — pre-training provides language understanding, English fine-tuning adds sentiment recognition patterns, and French adaptation leverages both. Each layer transfers relevant knowledge, reducing data needs at each subsequent stage.

distractors.B: Memorizing 100 examples would not generalize to new inputs. The model genuinely learned sentiment patterns transferable across languages.
distractors.C: French and English have different vocabularies and grammar. Transfer works because underlying sentiment concepts share structure across languages.
distractors.D: Required data depends heavily on task complexity and how much prior knowledge transfers. 100 examples only works because extensive prior training provided transferable foundations.

questions.scenario: A company uses the same base 70B model for three different products: customer support, code generation, and medical QA. Each product needs different fine-tuned behavior.
questions.stem: How does LoRA enable serving all three products efficiently?

options.text: Train three complete copies of the 70B model — one per product
Keep one frozen base model and swap small LoRA adapter weights per product — each adapter is only megabytes while the base model is hundreds of gigabytes
Combine all three fine-tuning datasets and train a single model that handles all products
Use prompt engineering for all three products without any fine-tuning

explanation.correct: LoRA produces small adapter weights (megabytes) for each task while keeping the base model frozen. One base model serves all products by loading different adapters — dramatically more efficient than maintaining three full model copies.

distractors.A: Three 70B copies requires 3x the storage and serving infrastructure. LoRA avoids this by sharing the base model.
distractors.C: Combined training risks catastrophic forgetting across domains and loses per-product optimization. Separate adapters maintain independence.
distractors.D: If prompting alone met all three products' needs, fine-tuning wouldn't be necessary. The scenario implies behavioral specialization beyond prompting.

questions.scenario: A team selects a foundation model from SageMaker JumpStart's model hub. They need to fine-tune it with a custom training script that implements their novel data augmentation strategy.
questions.stem: What does SageMaker JumpStart provide for this use case?

options.text: Only pre-built training scripts with no customization allowed
Pre-trained foundation models from a model hub with configurable training infrastructure and support for custom training scripts
Only inference endpoints — no training capability
Automatic model architecture design based on the dataset

explanation.correct: SageMaker JumpStart provides a model hub with pre-trained FMs, managed training infrastructure (GPU instances, distributed training), and support for both pre-built and custom training scripts — giving teams flexibility in their fine-tuning approach.

distractors.A: JumpStart supports custom scripts alongside pre-built options. Teams can bring their own training code while leveraging JumpStart's infrastructure.
distractors.C: JumpStart supports both fine-tuning (training) and deployment (inference). Training is a core capability, not just serving.
distractors.D: JumpStart provides existing architectures from the model hub. Architecture search/design is a separate concern (e.g., NAS).

questions.scenario: A team is preparing a fine-tuning dataset for a customer email response generator.
questions.stem: Which data preparation practices improve fine-tuning outcomes? (Select THREE)

options.text: Ensure examples cover diverse scenarios including edge cases, different tones, and various customer emotions
Remove contradictory or low-quality examples that could confuse the learning signal
Verify that labels accurately reflect the desired output for each input
Include identical duplicate examples to reinforce common patterns
Randomly shuffle labels to ensure the model doesn't memorize input-output pairs
Limit all examples to exactly 50 tokens regardless of natural variation

explanation.correct: Diverse coverage ensures generalization, removing contradictions provides clean learning signals, and accurate labels ensure the model learns correct patterns. All three directly improve what the model internalizes.

distractors.D: Duplicates can bias the model toward those specific patterns and waste training compute without adding information.
distractors.E: Shuffled labels provide random noise instead of learning signals. The model needs correct label-input associations to learn.
distractors.F: Artificial length restrictions remove natural variation. The model should learn from examples that reflect real-world input diversity.

questions.scenario: An ML team evaluates whether to use SageMaker JumpStart or Amazon Bedrock for fine-tuning.
questions.stem: In which situations would SageMaker JumpStart be preferred over Bedrock for fine-tuning? (Select TWO)

options.text: When the team needs full control over training hyperparameters, distributed training configuration, and custom training scripts
When the team wants to fine-tune open-source models not available in Bedrock's catalog
When the team wants zero infrastructure management and the simplest possible experience
When the team has no ML engineering expertise and needs a one-click solution
When fine-tuning must complete in under 5 minutes regardless of dataset size

explanation.correct: SageMaker provides full infrastructure control (hyperparameters, distributed config, custom scripts) and access to open-source model hubs beyond Bedrock's catalog. These capabilities justify the additional operational complexity.

distractors.C: Zero infrastructure management is Bedrock's strength, not SageMaker's. SageMaker requires more operational involvement.
distractors.D: Teams without ML engineering expertise benefit from Bedrock's managed simplicity. SageMaker's flexibility requires technical expertise to leverage.
distractors.E: Fine-tuning duration depends on data and model size, not the platform. Neither guarantees sub-5-minute completion.

questions.scenario: A platform team fine-tunes their model to follow instructions across summarization, classification, translation, code generation, and Q&A tasks.
questions.stem: What characterizes the resulting instruction-tuned model? (Select TWO)

options.text: It can generalize to new instructions beyond the specific tasks seen during fine-tuning
It maintains broader capability compared to single-task fine-tuned models because diverse training prevents catastrophic forgetting
It can only perform exactly the 5 tasks it was trained on and nothing else
It requires more inference compute than the base model due to multitask overhead
It has more parameters than the base model because tasks add layers

explanation.correct: Instruction-tuned models generalize to new instructions (they learn the meta-pattern of following instructions). The diverse training signal prevents over-specialization, maintaining general capability unlike single-task fine-tuning.

distractors.C: Instruction-tuned models generalize beyond training tasks. Learning to follow instructions transfers to novel instructions.
distractors.D: Model architecture is unchanged by fine-tuning. Inference compute is identical — only weights are different.
distractors.E: Fine-tuning doesn't add layers or parameters. The same architecture is used with updated weight values.

questions.scenario: A team trains a BERT model pre-trained on general English text, then fine-tunes it for detecting toxic comments in gaming forums. Despite the domain difference (general text vs gaming slang), the fine-tuned model achieves 91% accuracy with only 3,000 labeled gaming examples.
questions.stem: Why does the model perform well despite the domain gap between pre-training data and target task?

options.text: BERT memorized toxic gaming comments during pre-training
3,000 examples is always enough for perfect classification regardless of domain
Pre-trained language representations (grammar, sentiment, negation) transfer effectively — the model only needs to learn gaming-specific patterns from the 3,000 examples
The gaming forum data replaced all of BERT's pre-trained weights

explanation.correct: Transfer learning works because foundational language understanding (syntax, semantics, sentiment indicators, negation) transfers across domains. The model only needs task-specific examples to learn domain-specific patterns (gaming slang, context-dependent toxicity).

distractors.A: Pre-training was on general text. The model didn't memorize gaming content — it learned transferable language patterns.
distractors.B: Required examples depend on task complexity and domain gap. 3,000 worked here because strong pre-trained representations reduced data needs.
distractors.D: Fine-tuning with 3,000 examples updates weights incrementally. It doesn't replace all pre-trained knowledge — the model retains its language understanding.

questions.scenario: A company has 100,000 customer service transcripts they want to use for fine-tuning. However, 30% contain sensitive customer PII (names, account numbers, addresses) that must not be exposed to the model or the fine-tuning service.
questions.stem: What data preparation step must be completed before using this data for fine-tuning?

options.text: Remove or anonymize all PII from the transcripts through redaction, pseudonymization, or synthetic replacement before providing data to the training service
Train the model only on the 70% of transcripts without PII and discard the rest entirely
Configure the model to ignore PII tokens during training through a special inference parameter
Encrypt the training data — the model cannot learn from encrypted content

explanation.correct: PII must be redacted, anonymized, or replaced with synthetic equivalents before training. This preserves the conversational patterns needed for learning while removing sensitive information that should not be memorized by the model.

distractors.B: Discarding 30% of data loses valuable training signal. Anonymization preserves the examples while removing only the sensitive elements.
distractors.C: There is no inference parameter that prevents learning from specific tokens. The model processes all tokens in its training data equally.
distractors.D: Models cannot learn useful patterns from encrypted data. The data must be readable for training but should have PII removed beforehand.
